problem: Autonomous wheelchair navigation lacks social awareness (e.g. conversing groups, crossing pedestrians) and does not explain its decisions, so users and bystanders perceive low safety and trust. Existing systems either handle social awareness without transparency, or display what the chair will do but not why.
motivation: Powered wheelchair users bear high cognitive load, and crowded settings are where collisions are most frequent. An LLM can infer pedestrian intent and give natural-language rationales, offering both social reasoning and transparency, adapting the ROTE idea of hypothesizing others' behavior.
key_idea: Use an LLM to generate pedestrian-intent hypotheses (yield/rush/constant velocity) with rationales, score them by forward rollout for safety and progress, and feed the best one to a rule-based planner with social-bubble detours.
insight: The Ablation (same rule-based planner with the LLM disabled) differs from SAATT in all Scenario B metrics and in the Scenario C safety metrics, so the gains come from LLM intent and group reasoning, not the planner. Only the LLM lets the planner treat a conversing pair as a social bubble instead of two obstacles. Social awareness costs some efficiency: A* is faster and shorter in B and C.
method: LLM hypothesis generator: produces k=8 hypotheses per call (temperature 0.7), assigning each pedestrian yield/rush/constant-velocity with a natural-language rationale
Trigger scheduling: calls the LLM periodically (every 30 steps) or when a pedestrian is within 3.0 m, with at least 15 steps between calls

Rollout scorer: simulates each hypothesis for 30 steps with pedestrian speeds scaled (yield 0.2, rush 1.5), computes safety and progress scores, and picks the best by S_total with a collision penalty and a bubble penalty

Rule-based motion planner: intent-dependent slow/stop speed thresholds (yield thresholds larger), lateral steering away under rush, and a detour waypoint around a detected stationary group's social bubble
Pure pursuit controller: converts waypoints to angular velocity and acceleration commands with proportional gains
Transparency: the LLM's rationale is shown as text at each waypoint/refresh

setting.backbone: LLM (model unspecified in the text, used frozen as intent hypothesis generator) + rule-based planner and pure pursuit controller
setting.observation: 2D simulated states: wheelchair pose/velocity, pedestrian positions and velocities, obstacles, goal
setting.action_space: continuous differential-drive commands (linear acceleration, angular velocity) via pure pursuit toward waypoints
setting.simulator: custom 2D Python simulator (10 m x 10 m)
setting.privileged: Ground-truth pedestrian positions and velocities, and goal position, provided directly (no perception)

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark. Results in Table 1 are only statistical rankings (Friedman/Conover) with no numeric metric values; the paper gives no per-method means, only ranges in the text.
results: Across 3 custom scenarios (30 seeds each, 4 methods), SAATT ranked first in Collision Count, Minimum Pedestrian Distance and Bubble Intrusion Steps in scenarios B (conversing pair) and C (crossing pedestrian), beating A*, SFM and the Ablation. Success rates were near 100% for all methods with no significant difference. A* was faster in travel time (B, C) and shorter in path length (B), and had lower jerk in most scenarios.
limitations: Evaluated only in a simple custom 2D simulation with one or two pedestrians and no perception noise, and no real-robot or human-user study, so transparency and trust benefits are unverified
Only one SFM baseline as the social navigation representative; the LLM is not named, and LLM inference latency for real-time embedded deployment is unresolved
Pedestrians are treated only as repulsive, with no body-language cues or user preference fields; the social-efficiency trade-off costs longer travel time
